interactive.title: Circles from the radius
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens. Each shows circles drawn to scale: a circle rolled once along the ground, leaving a track as long as its rim, with its diameter laid under the track three times and a bit more; a circle cut into 16 wedges that open into a rough rectangle; a circle with the square on its radius split into 1 cm squares, and a radius you can drag; the ends of solid round wires, pipes, a shaft, a cable drum's barrel and a hatch cover. A size measured straight across is the diameter; one from the centre to the rim is the radius. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it.
interactive.ignores: All the sizes are example values, chosen so the numbers come out simply: the pipes, wires, shaft, drum and hatch cover. Answers use the calculator's π and are rounded to 2 decimal places. Sixteen wedges make only a rough rectangle; thinner wedges come closer to a true one. The wires are solid and round; this lesson does not work out a stranded cable's size from its outside width.

numbers.label: A circle rolled once lays down π diameters: 3 diameters and 0.14 of one, in step 1
A pipe 10 cm across: π × 10 = 31.42 cm round, not 2 × π × 10 = 62.83 cm or π × 5 = 15.71 cm, in step 2
A circle cut into 16 wedges, opened into a rough rectangle πr long and r tall, in step 3
A solid round wire 2 mm across: r = 1 mm and π × 1² = 3.14 mm², not π × 2² = 12.57 mm² or 2 × π × 1 = 6.28 mm, in step 5
Solid round wires 2 mm and 4 mm across: 3.14 mm² and 12.57 mm², four times as much, in step 6
A pipe 10 cm across outside and 8 cm inside: π × 5² − π × 4² = 78.54 − 50.27 = 28.27 cm², in step 7
A pipe 12 cm across outside and 10 cm inside: 113.10 − 78.54 = 34.56 cm², not π × 1² = 3.14 cm² or 138.23 cm², in step 8
A round shaft's end of 28.27 cm²: 28.27 ÷ π = 9.00, so r = 3 cm and it is 6 cm across, not 3 cm or 18 cm, in step 9
A cable drum's barrel of radius 30 cm: 2 × π × 30 = 188.50 cm round, not 94.25 cm or 376.99 cm, in step 10
One solid wire 4 mm across, 12.57 mm², against two 2 mm across, 2 × 3.14 = 6.28 mm², in step 11
A round hatch cover 0.6 m across: π × 0.3² = 0.28 m², not 1.13 m² or 1.88 m, in step 12

explain.text:
A circle is measured from its centre. The radius runs from the centre to the rim, and the diameter goes straight across through the centre, so it is two radii. Roll a circle once and the track it leaves, the [[circumference]], is just over 3 diameters long, a number called π, about 3.14. Bitesize gives it as C = πd,[^1] and since d = 2r, that is also C = 2πr. For the area, cut the circle into thin wedges and lay them top to tail. NCTM's lesson notes that the rough rectangle they make is half the circumference long, or πr,[^2] and it stands one radius tall, so the area is πr × r, which is πr².

The area rule needs the radius, so halve a diameter first; for the way round, use πd with a diameter or 2πr with a radius. NCTM lists difficulty using C, d and r,[^3] and the slip costs a lot. A solid round wire 2 mm across has r = 1 mm, so its cross-section is π × 1² = 3.14 mm², but π × 2² gives 12.57 mm², four times too much. Because the radius is squared, a solid round wire twice as wide across has four times the cross-section, as the Bureau of Standards' copper wire tables put it, cross section varies with the square of the diameter.[^4] A ring, or [[annulus]], such as a pipe's end, is the whole circle less the hole, so work out each with πr² before taking one from the other. To go back from an area to a width, divide by π, take the square root to get r, then double it.

**Circumference is πd, or 2πr from the radius, and area is πr², which needs the radius, so halve a diameter first. Twice the width of a round wire gives four times its cross-section, and a ring is the whole circle less the hole.**

practice.text:
**Rule of thumb:** Find the radius first, halving a diameter if that is what you have. The way round is 2πr, a length, and the area is πr², in square units. For a ring, work out both circles with πr², then take the hole from the whole. To find a width from an area, divide by π, take the square root and double it.

**Worked example:** A pipe is 10 cm across outside and 8 cm across inside. Halve both, so the radii are 5 cm and 4 cm. The whole circle is π × 5² = 78.54 cm² and the hole is π × 4² = 50.27 cm², so the metal ring is 78.54 − 50.27 = 28.27 cm².

**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up the diameter and the radius, a difficulty NCTM lists with C, d and r.[^3] A 2 mm diameter put into πr² gives 12.57 mm², four times the true 3.14 mm². A pipe 10 cm across is π × 10 = 31.42 cm round, not 2 × π × 10 = 62.83 cm. A shaft whose radius works out at 3 cm is 6 cm across, not 3 cm.

interactive.html:
Circles and rings drawn to scale and measured across or from the centre, with example pipes, wires, a shaft, a drum and a hatch cover.

Circumference is 2πr and area is πr², both from the radius. The sizes are example values.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is that a circle's wedges open into a rough rectangle πr long and r tall, so its area is πr², and that the area rule needs the radius, so a diameter is halved first (the way round is πd from a diameter or 2πr from a radius), and that twice the width makes four times the area, when you roll circles out, open one up, drag its radius and lift a ring's hole out.

checks.label: The circumference of a circle is given by the formula C = πd: the circle rolled once lays a track π of its diameters long, three of them and a bit; the pipe measured across is π times that width round, and the drum given its radius is π times twice the radius round

The length of the rectangle is equal to half the circumference of the circle, or πr: the opened wedges lie top to tail in a rectangle within a hundredth of πr long and within a fiftieth of r tall, so its area is πr × r, half of each wedge pointing up and half down

The cross section varies with the square of the diameter: a solid round wire twice as wide across has four times the cross-section, so wire B holds four of wire A's squares, and one wire twice as wide has twice the cross-section of two narrow ones together

Difficulty using the variables C, d and r: each wrong answer offered that mixes them up is exactly what the mix-up gives, a width used as a radius, half the width in πd, a radius doubled into twice π r, a radius given as the width, and each has its own hint

Twice the radius makes four times the area: at r = 1, 2, 3 and 4 cm the square on the radius holds 1, 4, 9 and 16 unit squares, and the circle covers π of them, 3.14, 12.57, 28.27 and 50.27 cm², drawn to scale

A ring is the whole circle less the hole, each from its own radius: 78.54 − 50.27 = 28.27 cm² and 113.10 − 78.54 = 34.56 cm², the rounded parts giving the rounded whole, while taking the radii away first gives π × 1² = 3.14 cm²
Each puzzle's answer is worked out from its rule: 31.42 cm, 3.14 mm², 4 times, 34.56 cm², 6 cm, 188.50 cm, the one 4 mm wire and 0.28 m²; the shaft's 28.27 cm² ÷ π is 9.00, so r = 3 cm

Each puzzle accepts only its own answer, and each wrong answer it offers is the one a slip gives, shown in the warning colour with its own hint: a width as a radius, half way round, a radius doubled twice, the way round for the area, twice as wide taken as twice the area, the radii taken away first, the radius as the width, r² without its root

Before an answer, nothing in a puzzle's picture gives it away: its readout asks "?" (the shaft's shows only the area given), no radius square, no radius, no lifted hole, no rolled track and nothing in the warning colour
Every screen, finished, keeps its labels inside the picture and clear of each other, for every answer, right or wrong, and at every radius Dan can drag

Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion within 2.5 s and a slip within 1 s; parts start at least 0.45 s apart and counted steps at least 0.2 s apart

applied.problem: "Both rules start from the radius" and the bold "πd ... both from the radius" are not true as worded: C = πd starts from the diameter, as screen 2 itself works it (π × 10). Also "a wire 2 mm across" must be solid and round for π × 1² to give its cross-section.

It describes things the screens do not draw: screen 4 has no grid of 1 cm squares (only the square on the radius is split into 1 cm squares), and screen 1 lays the diameter under the track three times and a bit, not beside it.
